CausalChain: Viral infection/stress -> Upregulation of demethylases (e.g., ALKBH3) -> Site-specific tRNA demethylation -> Increased susceptibility to ANG-mediated cleavage -> Accumulation of specific tRF-5 fragments -> Selective loading into noncanonical Argonaute complexes (Ago1, Ago3, Ago4) -> Reprogrammed mRNA translation and stability -> Suppressed antiviral responses and enhanced viral replication/oncogenesis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that viral infection-induced stress leads to an upregulation of specific tRNA demethylases such as ALKBH3, which catalyze targeted demethylation on tRNAs. This demethylation enhances the structural susceptibility of tRNAs to cleavage by angiogenin (ANG), culminating in an increased production of distinct tRNA-derived fragments (notably tRF-5 fragments). These tRF-5 molecules are selectively incorporated into noncanonical Argonaute complexes (Ago1, Ago3, Ago4), thereby orchestrating a reprogramming of the cell’s mRNA translation and stability networks. This targeted regulatory shift undermines host antiviral defenses and reinforces viral replication, concurrently activating oncogenic pathways as observed in cancer-associated tRF dysregulation. Our approach employs state-of-the-art technologies, including CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene editing, RIP-seq, and ribosome profiling, to precisely dissect and therapeutically target each step of this pathway.
Abstract: Viral infections impose cellular stress that can recalibrate the epitranscriptomic landscape of tRNAs, thereby facilitating a cascade of molecular events critical for viral propagation and potential oncogenic transformation. In this study, we propose that stress-induced upregulation of demethylases (e.g., ALKBH3) triggers precise demethylation events on tRNAs, rendering them more susceptible to cleavage by enzymes such as ANG. The resultant accumulation of specific tRF-5 fragments is then selectively loaded into noncanonical Argonaute complexes (Ago1, Ago3, Ago4), which reprogram mRNA translation and stability. This reprogramming dampens host antiviral responses while favoring viral replication and oncogenic processes. Leveraging contemporary tools such as CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, high-throughput RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq), and ribosome profiling, our framework not only elucidates a coherent molecular mechanism but also paves the way for targeted therapeutic interventions in both viral infections and cancer.
Orignal_vs_New: The new hypothesis retains the original causal chain of events—viral infection leading to stress-induced tRNA demethylation, followed by enhanced cleavage of tRNAs, accumulation of tRF fragments, selective Argonaute loading, and subsequent reprogramming of mRNA translation—but refines each step with greater specificity. It explicitly identifies the tRF subtype (tRF-5) and names the Argonaute complexes (Ago1, Ago3, Ago4) involved, thus aligning closely with observed regulatory mechanisms. Furthermore, the revised hypothesis incorporates modern experimental technologies (CRISPR, RIP-seq, ribosome profiling) to enhance practical implementability and facilitate targeted therapeutic strategies against viral replication and cancer. This new formulation bridges the original theoretical framework with actionable, empirically testable experiments, thereby strengthening its novelty and translational potential.
